title: Festival Darling Max, Min and Meowzaki Finally Hits Indian Theatres
excerpt: Padmakumar Narasimhamurthy's multigenerational dramedy about a Mumbai family, a breakup, and a cat named after Hayao Miyazaki arrives in cinemas after a four-year international festival run.
body:
• Max, Min and Meowzaki opens in Indian cinemas on July 24 after a four-year journey that began at Busan International Film Festival in 2022
  • The ensemble dramedy starring Adil Hussain, Medha Shankr, and Siddharth Menon follows three generations of a Mumbai family dealing with breakups, grief, and forgiveness
  • Distributed by Platoon One Films, the movie won awards at festivals from Palm Springs to Berlin, Stuttgart, and Osaka before getting its India theatrical release
  • Director Padmakumar Narasimhamurthy calls it "a film about forgiveness, which is very essential for this era"

A Cat, a Breakup, and Three Generations

https://youtube.com/watch?v=53wRc9Cxd5A

Max, Min and Meowzaki, one of the most festival-travelled Indian films of recent years, opens in theatres across India on July 24 — nearly four years after its world premiere at the Busan International Film Festival in 2022.

Written and directed by Padmakumar Narasimhamurthy, whose earlier feature A Billion Colour Story drew critical acclaim, the Hindi and English-language film follows three generations of the Mahadevan family in Mumbai. At its center is a young couple — Max (Siddharth Menon), a voice actor and rock singer, and Min (Medha Shankr), a filmmaker — whose relationship unravels just as life demands they hold on. Their shared cat, Meowzaki, named after Japanese animation master Hayao Miyazaki, becomes an unlikely fulcrum around which questions of custody, attachment, and moving on revolve.

The film extends well beyond the central breakup. Max is simultaneously grieving the death of his mother Vasudha (Gitanjali Rao) to cancer. His father Ramesh (Adil Hussain), a conservative Tamil Brahmin businessman, struggles with unresolved grief and a strained relationship with his son, eventually seeking help from a healer named Dhaara (Mandira Bedi). Ramesh's father, played by Nasser, and a warmly drawn cat-sitter named Carol (Vidhatri Bandi) round out the ensemble, alongside Nafisa Ali.

"In all of us, somewhere or the other, there is a wound. This film understands individual human fallibilities, wounds, vulnerabilities and flaws. It's a film about forgiveness, which is very essential for this era."

— Padmakumar Narasimhamurthy, Director

Four Years on the Festival Circuit

The film's path to Indian theatres has been unusually long. After premiering at Busan in 2022, it was selected for the Best of Fest programme at Palm Springs International Film Festival and screened at the International Film Festival of Kerala and the Golden Horse Film Festival. It went on to earn audience honours in Sonoma, San Francisco, and Osaka, and won best feature awards at Stuttgart, Cincinnati, Berlin's Indo-German Film Week, and RIFFA in Canada. Its UK premiere came at the BFI Southbank during the London Indian Film Festival in June 2023.

The India release is handled by Platoon One Films, founded by Shiladitya Bora, which has been positioning itself as a champion of non-formulaic Indian cinema.

"We're building India's A24, one uncompromised film at a time. Theatrical isn't dead. It just needs films worth leaving the house for."

— Shiladitya Bora, Founder, Platoon One Films

What Critics Are Saying

Early reviews have been broadly positive, with critics praising the film's emotional ambition even where they note imperfections. Asian Movie Pulse described it as "a lighthearted but timely survey of social issues in India," highlighting Narasimhamurthy's willingness to tackle childhood and domestic trauma within a comedy-drama framework. The review singled out Adil Hussain's portrayal of Ramesh as a standout, and praised Vidhatri Bandi's "bright but slightly world-weary" Carol.

At 140-plus minutes, the runtime has drawn some criticism — Asian Movie Pulse noted the film "struggles to hold" at that length, though "one retracts blame when thinking on the script's thematic ambitions." The film's willingness to address communal prejudice, gender norms, and intergenerational pain within an accessible format has been noted by multiple reviewers, with South Asian Herald calling it "a sweet slice-of-life recipe."

Produced by Samiksha and Shael Oswal of SSO Productions, the film benefits from what Bollywood Hungama called a "catchy and unobtrusive soundtrack" that lets character interactions drive the mood.

A Film for the Diaspora Conversation

For diaspora audiences, Max, Min and Meowzaki touches familiar terrain: the generational gulf between traditional conservatism and the more fluid identities of younger Indians, the difficulty of grief across cultural expectations, and the slow work of family reconciliation. The Mahadevans' story — a Tamil Brahmin family navigating therapy, interfaith relationships, and changing gender dynamics in contemporary Mumbai — mirrors conversations playing out in Indian households from London to the Bay Area.

As lead actor Siddharth Menon told ANI, "If families watch it together, the conversations that should happen at home will begin and misunderstandings will start getting cleared."

Looking Ahead

No OTT release date has been announced. In a Bollywood landscape dominated by franchise spectacles and high-concept thrillers, Max, Min and Meowzaki offers something rarer: a quiet, character-driven film that trusts its audience to sit with messy, complicated feelings — and a very professional cat named Radha.
nri_angle: The film's exploration of generational divides, interfaith relationships, and evolving family dynamics mirrors conversations in Indian diaspora households worldwide.
